title: Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV: Mapping the Milky Way, Nearby Galaxies, and the Distant Universe
abstract: Abstract We describe the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV (SDSS-IV), a project encompassing three major spectroscopic programs. The Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment 2 (APOGEE-2) is observing hundreds of thousands of Milky Way stars at high resolution and high signal-to-noise ratios in the near-infrared. The Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey is obtaining spatially resolved spectroscopy for thousands of nearby galaxies (median ). The extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) is mapping the galaxy, quasar, and neutral gas distributions between and 3.5 to constrain cosmology using baryon acoustic oscillations, redshift space distortions, and the shape of the power spectrum. Within eBOSS, we are conducting two major subprograms: the SPectroscopic IDentification of eROSITA Sources (SPIDERS), investigating X-ray AGNs and galaxies in X-ray clusters, and the Time Domain Spectroscopic Survey (TDSS), obtaining spectra of variable sources. All programs use the 2.5 m Sloan Foundation Telescope at the Apache Point Observatory; observations there began in Summer 2014. APOGEE-2 also operates a second near-infrared spectrograph at the 2.5 m du Pont Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory, with observations beginning in early 2017. Observations at both facilities are scheduled to continue through 2020. In keeping with previous SDSS policy, SDSS-IV provides regularly scheduled public data releases; the first one, Data Release 13, was made available in 2016 July.
summary:
Title: Groundbreaking Milky Way Mapping Project Unveiled by Astronomers

In an unprecedented survey, a team of international astronomers have launched Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV (SDSS-IV), the latest phase of an ongoing project that aims to map the Milky Way, nearby galaxies, and the distant universe. The project encompasses three major spectroscopic programs, including APOGEE-2, MaNGA, eBOSS, SPIDERS, and TDSS.

APOGEE-2 observes hundreds of thousands of Milky Way stars at high resolution and signal-to-noise ratios in the near-infrared, while MaNGA focuses on spatially resolved spectroscopy for thousands of nearby galaxies. eBOSS, the core program, maps the distribution of galaxies, quasars, and neutral gas between redshifts 0.6 and 3.5 to construct a detailed cosmic map using baryon acoustic oscillations, redshift space distortions, and power spectrum shapes.

These efforts will provide researchers with invaluable data to unravel the mysteries of our universe's past, present, and future. Public data releases have commenced with Data Release 13 in 2016, and observations at both the Apache Point Observatory and Las Campanas Observatory are expected to continue through 2020.

title: THE SPITZER c2d LEGACY RESULTS: STAR-FORMATION RATES AND EFFICIENCIES; EVOLUTION AND LIFETIMES
abstract: The c2d Spitzer Legacy project obtained images and photometry with both IRAC and MIPS instruments for five large, nearby molecular clouds. Three of the clouds were also mapped in dust continuum emission at 1.1 mm, and optical spectroscopy has been obtained for some clouds. This paper combines inFormation drawn from studies of individual clouds into a combined and updated statistical analysis of star-Formation rates and efficiencies, numbers and lifetimes for spectral energy distribution (SED) classes, and clustering properties. Current star-Formation efficiencies range from 3% to 6%; if star Formation continues at current rates for 10 Myr, efficiencies could reach 15-30%. Star-Formation rates and rates per unit area vary from cloud to cloud; taken together, the five clouds are producing about 260 M(circle dot) of stars per Myr. The star-Formation surface density is more than an order of magnitude larger than would be predicted from the Kennicutt relation used in extragalactic studies, reflecting the fact that those relations apply to larger scales, where more diffuse matter is included in the gas surface density. Measured against the dense gas probed by the maps of dust continuum emission, the efficiencies are much higher, with stellar masses similar to masses of dense gas, and the current stock of dense cores would be exhausted in 1.8 Myr on average. Nonetheless, star Formation is still slow compared to that expected in a free-fall time, even in the dense cores. The derived lifetime for the Class I phase is 0.54 Myr, considerably longer than some estimates. Similarly, the lifetime for the Class 0 SED class, 0.16 Myr, with the notable exception of the Ophiuchus cloud, is longer than early estimates. If photometry is corrected for estimated extinction before calculating class indicators, the lifetimes drop to 0.44 Myr for Class I and to 0.10 for Class 0. These lifetimes assume a continuous flow through the Class II phase and should be considered median lifetimes or half-lives. Star Formation is highly concentrated to regions of high extinction, and the youngest objects are very strongly associated with dense cores. The great majority (90%) of young stars lie within loose clusters with at least 35 members and a stellar density of 1 M(circle dot) pc(-3). Accretion at the sound speed from an isothermal sphere over the lifetime derived for the Class I phase could build a star of about 0.25 M(circle dot), given an efficiency of 0.3. Building larger mass stars by using higher mass accretion rates could be problematic, as our data confirm and aggravate the "luminosity problem" for protostars. At a given T(bol), the values for L(bol) are mostly less than predicted by standard infall models and scatter over several orders of magnitude. These results strongly suggest that accretion is time variable, with prolonged periods of very low accretion. Based on a very simple model and this sample of sources, half the mass of a star would be accreted during only 7% of the Class I lifetime, as represented by the eight most luminous objects.
summary:
**New Research Reveals Star Formation Rates and Efficiencies**

A groundbreaking study by renowned astrophysicists led by Neal J. Evans has provided fresh insights into star formation rates and efficiencies in five nearby molecular clouds, published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series.

The research combines data from various sources – including images, photometry, spectral studies, and 1.1mm dust continuum emission mapping – to arrive at a comprehensive statistical analysis. The findings reveal that current star formation efficiencies range between 3% and 6%, potentially doubling within 10 million years if the rate remains constant.

The research highlights differences in star-formation rates across clouds, with an overall production of about 260 solar masses per million years among the five studied stellar nurseries. The investigators propose that current efficiencies, despite being much lower than what would be expected in a free-fall time, could increase significantly given more rapid star formation within dense cores.

The study reveals intriguing details about the lifetimes and evolution phases of young stars. For instance, the lifetime for the Class I phase is found to be 0.54 million years, which exceeds some prior estimates. Similarly, the lifetime for the Class 0 SED class (0.16 million years) is longer than earlier predictions, except for the Ophiuchus cloud.

The research indicates that accretion – a process central to protostar development – may be variable over time, and prolonged periods of lower accretion rates could account for discrepancies observed in standard infall models regarding luminosity.

In addition, the study shows strong associations between youngest stars and dense cores, revealing that star formation is highly concentrated in regions of high extinction. The majority of young stars lie within loose clusters containing at least 35 members and a stellar density of one solar mass per cubic parsec.
